26170fea140c96fe9089fbf289213e59.overview: Lars von Trier shook up the film world when he premiered Antichrist at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival. In this graphic psychodrama, a grief-stricken man and woman—a searing Willem Dafoe and Cannes best actress winner Charlotte Gainsbourg—retreat to their cabin deep in the woods after the accidental death of their infant son, only to find terror and violence at the hands of nature and, ultimately, each other. But this most confrontational work yet from one of contemporary cinema’s most controversial artists is no mere provocation. It is a visually sublime, emotionally ravaging journey to the darkest corners of the possessed human mind; a disturbing battle of the sexes that pits rational psychology against age-old superstition; and a profoundly effective horror film.

262e44e7b4257f1a2419171d3540a137.overview: Brian De Palma ascended to the highest ranks of American suspense filmmaking with this virtuoso, explicit erotic thriller. At once tongue in cheek and scary as hell, Dressed to Kill revolves around the grisly murder of a woman in Manhattan and how her psychiatrist, her brainiac teenage son, and the prostitute who witnessed the crime try to piece together what happened while the killer remains at large. With its masterfully executed scenes of horror, voluptuous camera work, and passionate score, Dressed to Kill is a veritable symphony of terror, enhanced by vivid performances by Angie Dickinson, Michael Caine, and Nancy Allen.

26346273038f00cbd51440219ababd08.overview: For decades, journalist Jep Gambardella has charmed and seduced his way through the glittering nightlife of Rome. Since the legendary success of his only novel, he has been a permanent fixture in the city’s literary and elite social circles. But on his sixty-fifth birthday, Jep unexpectedly finds himself taking stock of his life, turning his cutting wit on himself and his contemporaries, and looking past the lavish nightclubs, parties, and cafés to find Rome itself, in all its monumental glory: a timeless landscape of absurd, exquisite beauty. Featuring sensuous cinematography, a lush score, and an award-winning central performance by the great Toni Servillo, this transporting experience by the brilliant Italian director Paolo Sorrentino is a breathtaking Felliniesque tale of decadence and lost love.

2637972b28d9ad7e9fcefa242f3239ed.afih:
Opening credits note: “The Company dedicates this picture to Dorothy Stratten.”

End credits include the following statements: “Particular Thanks to: George and Ira Gershwin, The New York City Mayor’s Office for Motion Pictures and Television, The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, Sikorsky Aircraft, Dav-El Limousines” and “We thank the people of Manhattan, on whose island this picture was filmed.”

The 7 Dec 1979 DV announced that Peter Bogdanovich would write, produce and direct They All Laughed for Time-Life Films, and the film would be released domestically by 20th Century-Fox, which had a three year deal with Time-Life for domestic theatrical distribution. Time-Life financed the $7.5 million film on its own and retained all other rights. Reportedly, the company had not set up “network prelicensing or other deals,” speculating that the film would be successful at the box-office and Time-Life could negotiate higher prices. David Susskind was to executive produce the film, however, as noted in an article in the 4 Nov 1981 Var, Bogdanovich and Susskind had a “falling out” and Bogdanovich “inherited” the film from Susskind, who did not receive onscreen credit.

A 4 Apr 1980 HR brief stated that principal photography began 31 Mar 1980 in New York City. According to the 13 Dec 1981 LAT, Bogdanovich and actress Dorothy Stratten, a former Playboy Playmate of the Year, fell in love during filming and planned to marry. However, on 14 Aug 1980, after the completion of principal photography, Stratten was murdered by her estranged husband, Paul Snider, who then committed suicide.

After completion of principal photography on the film, Time-Life Films shut down, citing that the company’s first two films, 1980’s Loving Couples and 1981’s Fort Apache, The Bronx (see entries), “failed to perform well enough.” The 24 Aug 1981 LAHExam reported that They All Laughed sat on the shelf at 20th Century-Fox for more than a year, before the distributor test-marketed the film. As noted in the 4 Nov 1981 Var, the test screenings were in Phoenix, AZ, Providence, RI, and Minneapolis, MN, in Aug 1981. Bogdanovich claimed the film received “good word-of-mouth and steady grosses for four weeks.” However, 20th Century-Fox felt the test screenings were “not encouraging,” and pulled the film from distribution. An item in the 1 Sep 1981 HR announced They All Laughed would be the opening night presentation at the Venice International Film Festival, screening out of competition on 2 Sep 1981. The 23 Sep 1981 DV noted the film was well received at the Venice and Deauville film festivals, and a release of the film might be imminent.

As tracked in articles in the 2 Oct 1981 DV, 4 Nov 1981 Var, the 13 Dec 1981 LAT, the 27 May 1982 DV, the 28 Oct 1982 DV, and the 19 Dec 1985 LAT, Bogdanovich was unhappy with 20th Century-Fox’s distribution plans. Feeling the film would not get the attention it deserved, Bogdanovich decided to purchase domestic distribution rights. Time-Life reimbursed 20th Century-Fox for the test screening costs, reportedly between $350,000-$500,000. Bogdanovich formed the production-distribution company Moon Pictures, and then partnered with the film’s foreign distributor, Producers Sales Organization (PSO), to make a deal with Time-Life for domestic distribution. Bogdanovich guaranteed to repay Time-Life’s $8.6 million financing. The company would continue to retain participation in the film after full reimbursement, and the Time-Life logo would appear on the film prints. A benefit for a country & western music foundation in Nashville, TN, was planned for 18 Nov 1981, followed by the film’s release at Nashville’s Melrose Theatre. On 20 Nov 1981, it would be released in New York City at the Cinema Studio 1 and the Lincoln Plaza 1, at two theaters in Kansas City, MO, and single theaters in Scottsdale, AZ, and Portland, OR. Openings in Seattle, WA, and Vancouver, BC, on 11 Dec 1981 would be followed by the 18 Dec 1981 Los Angeles, CA, release at the Beverly Hills Music Hall. Bogdanovich hoped for a wide release in Jan 1982, but other Christmas releases “precluded long holdovers and new engagements.”

The 12 Jan 1982 LAT reported that Bogdanovich made a deal with the Z Channel to air two telecasts of They All Laughed during the channel’s screenings of recent films hoping for Academy Award nominations. However, Bogdanovich did not hold pay-TV rights to the film. Despite announcements in the TV Guide and TV Times and advertisements on the Z Channel, the airings were canceled by Time Inc., which planned to air it on their subsidiary, Home Box Office (HBO).

According to the 27 May 1982 DV, Bogdanovich stated that it cost him $2.5 million to release the film domestically, however, he closed Moon Picture’s six-month old distribution arm, in part because it was difficult for an independent distributor to get paid by theaters in a timely manner. Bogdanovich also noted that a more expensive advertising campaign was necessary to lure audiences. He made a deal with UA Classics to handle advertising and domestic distribution of the film. Tele-pictures Inc. had nontheatrical rights, HBO had cable rights, and Bogdanovich planned to sell network television rights at a later date.

The 28 Oct 1982 DV reported Time-Life filed a lawsuit in Los Angeles Federal court against Moon Pictures, Bogdanovich and Copo De Oro Productions, “his long-standing firm.” The suit asked for at least $150,000, alleging Moon Pictures failed to make the “necessary” 30 Jun 1982 payment, even after being given an extension until 15 Sep 1982. The suit also requested a determination that Bogdanovich’s company had no further rights to act as the film’s domestic distributor. The outcome of the lawsuit is unknown as of Feb 2015.

Items in the 5 Jun 1985 LAHExam and the 10 Jun 1985 People reported Bogdanovich was considering re-scoring and re-releasing the film. Bogdanovich hoped to add several Bruce Springsteen songs, but admitted he had not made a deal with Springsteen.

The 19 Dec 1985 LAT reported Bogdanovich filed for Chapter 7 federal bankruptcy, and his business office stated the “attempt to market and distribute the film as a memorial to Dorothy Stratten” failed, leaving Bogdanovich more than $6.6 million in debt against assets of approximately $1.5 million. Bogdanovich invested nearly $5 million in the film, but the box-office gross was “well under” $1 million and he received less than half of that.

They All Laughed marked the feature film debuts of actors Blaine Novak, Linda MacEwen and Sean Ferrer, who is the son of the film’s star Audrey Hepburn. The 20 Nov 1981 NYT review reported that actress Patti Hansen also made her feature film debut, but Hansen appeared in 1979’s Rich Kids (see entry).
2637972b28d9ad7e9fcefa242f3239ed.overview: New York's Odyssey Detective Agency is hired by two different clients to follow two women suspected of infidelity. Ladies' man John Russo trails Angela Niotes, the elegant wife of a wealthy Italian industrialist, while Charles Rutledge and Arthur Brodsky follow Dolores Martin, the beautiful young wife of a jealous husband. Their respective cases are complicated when John falls for Angela, and Charles falls for Dolores.
2637972b28d9ad7e9fcefa242f3239ed.tagline: Some of them promised they'd never fall in love.

263b4a1d6c8309bc91d8dc4cfde76b48.overview: Marina, 23, is growing up with her architect father in a prototype factory town by the sea. Finding the human species strange and repellent, she keeps her distance...that is until a stranger comes to town and challenges her to a foosball duel, on her own table. Her father, meanwhile, ritualistically prepares for his exit from the 20th century, which he considers to be "overrated."

264c6cb63939b836ede5ffd9509496ff.afih:
An item in the 4 September 1915 Reel Life announced that W. C. Fields had been signed by Mutual Film to star in a series of comedies. The first, The Pool Sharks, "will bring into play Mr. Fields' famed facility with the cue." The appearance of the internationally-famous Fields, who was under exclusive contract to impresario Florenz Ziegfeld, assured viewers that Mutual was "making good" on its promise of its "new 'all-star, all-feature, $8,000,000 program." Pool Sharks, based on one of Fields' stage routines, was his first motion picture. He would make only one other film, His Lordship's Dilemma, for Gaumount Mutual, and not return to motion pictures until 1924.

Mutual advertisements in the 18 September 1915 and 2 October 1915 issues of Moving Picture World described W.C. Fields as "The Popular Comedian of Ziegfeld Follies" and called Pool Sharks a "Casino Star Comedy."

The 23 October 1915 Motion Picture News reported that Pool Sharks and another "Casino Comedy" had already been filmed, and a third was in production.

Filming was done at Gaumont's studios in Flushing Meadows Park, Queens, NY.

The 2 October Motion Picture News gave this review: "Admirers of Fields will find his scene work neither as subtle nor as laughable as his stage performances. There is plenty of good fun in the picture, however, and much of the 'business' is new." The 30 October 1915 Moving Picture World added: "An eccentric comedy number with amusing spots in it. W. C. Fields, the well-known juggler, is featured assisted by Budd Ross. A comedy pool game is part of the picture. This contains some good nonsense."

Prints commonly in circulation have replaced main and subtitles, and added a "Copyright Raymond Rohauer, MCMLXVIII [1968]" notice. This copyright only covers newly created material, such as the new titles and perhaps a re-ordering of scenes.
264c6cb63939b836ede5ffd9509496ff.overview: W. C. Fields’s prolific career placed him at the forefront of slapstick comedy. Gathered here are six gems that feature the comic genius at his peak: The Golf Specialist, Pool Sharks (silent), The Pharmacist, The Fatal Glass of Beer, The Barber Shop, and, of course, the notorious The Dentist. This unique collection will delight new generations of viewers with Fields’s hilariously sardonic routines.
264c6cb63939b836ede5ffd9509496ff.tagline: Two romantic rivals play a game of pool

26ab6cb78d12e84b276f60278ec1b82f.afih:
According to a 4 Oct 1949 LAT news item, many scenes in this film were shot in Romanoff's café, a well-known Hollywood restaurant. Modern sources, however, report that the film was largely shot on a studio sound stage, and "Paul's Restaurant" was merely "inspired" by Romanoff's.

The courtyard apartment scenes were filmed at Columbia Studios, but the set was a duplication of the real courtyard from the Villa Primavera Apartments at 1300-1308 North Harper Avenue in West Hollywood, where director Nicholas Ray had lived during his early days in Hollywood. When Humphrey Bogart's character, “Dix,” tells his visitor, “Mildred Atkinson,” to catch a taxi just around the corner on Santa Monica Boulevard, the geography is correct. However, the story implies that "Dix" lived in Beverly Hills, because he is taken to Beverly Hills City Hall at 455 North Rexford Drive after Mildred's death.

According to modern sources, Ginger Rogers was considered for the role of "Laurel Gray."

During filming Nicholas Ray separated from his wife, Gloria Grahame. Ray has been quoted in modern sources as stating that if the studio had known about their separation, he would have been fired, so they kept it secret. The film depicts a realistic romance between two disillusioned people. "Dix" tells "Laurel" that his idea of two people in love is a guy cutting grapefruit and a girl, "sitting over there," half-asleep. At the end of the film "Laurel" quotes a line from his script that reveals "Dix" as a romantic: "I was born when you kissed me. I died when you left me. I lived a few weeks while you loved me."

Hadda Brooks, who performed the uncredited song “I Hadn't Anyone Till You” at a piano bar, was listed last in the credits. She had been a local recording artist known as “Queen of the Boogie.”

In the original novel by Dorothy B. Hughes, "Dix" was the murderer.
26ab6cb78d12e84b276f60278ec1b82f.overview: When a gifted but washed-up screenwriter with a hair-trigger temper—Humphrey Bogart, in a revelatory, vulnerable performance—becomes the prime suspect in a brutal Tinseltown murder, the only person who can supply an alibi for him is a seductive neighbor (Gloria Grahame) with her own troubled past. The emotionally charged In a Lonely Place, freely adapted from a Dorothy B. Hughes thriller, is a brilliant, turbulent mix of suspenseful noir and devastating melodrama, fueled by powerhouse performances. An uncompromising tale of two people desperate to love yet struggling with their demons and each other, this is one of the greatest films of the 1950s, and a benchmark in the career of the classic Hollywood auteur Nicholas Ray.
26ab6cb78d12e84b276f60278ec1b82f.tagline: The Bogart suspense picture with the surprise finish!

26b9a263a46263b7b0174c354075ded5.overview:
With his third feature film, The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog, Alfred Hitchcock took a major step toward greatness and made what he would come to consider his true directorial debut. This haunting silent thriller tells the tale of a mysterious young man (matinee idol Ivor Novello) who takes up residence at a London boardinghouse just as a killer known as the Avenger descends upon the city, preying on blonde women. The film is animated by the palpable energy of a young stylist at play, decisively establishing the director’s formal and thematic obsessions. In this release, The Lodger is accompanied by Downhill, another silent from 1927 that explores Hitchcock’s “wrong man” trope, also headlined by Novello—making for a double feature that reveals the master of the macabre as he was just coming into his own.

The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog was restored by the BFI National Archive. Principal restoration funding provided by the Hollywood Foreign Press Association, The Film Foundation, and Simon W. Hessel. Additional funding provided by the British Board of Film Classification, Deluxe 142, Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, and Ian and Beth Mill. New score commissioned by Network Releasing in partnership with the BFI.

26c87c81146476f55ccaffbd70e8ecb7.overview: The staff of an American magazine based in France puts out its last issue, with stories featuring an artist sentenced to life imprisonment, student riots, and a kidnapping resolved by a chef.
26c87c81146476f55ccaffbd70e8ecb7.tagline: Bringing the world to Kansas, one eccentric story at a time.

26fb9351e01d638a0ddc2dcbc4741bc8.overview: An exquisitely understated ode to the thrill of romantic possibility, the inaugural installment of The Before Trilogy opens with a chance encounter between two solitary young strangers. After they hit it off on a train bound for Vienna, the Paris university student Celine and the scrappy American tourist Jesse impulsively decide to spend a day together before he returns to the U.S. the next morning. As the pair roam the streets of the stately city, Richard Linklater’s tenderly observant gaze captures the uncertainty and intoxication of young love, from the first awkward stirrings of attraction to the hopeful promise that Celine and Jesse make upon their inevitable parting.
26fb9351e01d638a0ddc2dcbc4741bc8.tagline: Can the greatest romance of your life last only one night?
